..
Issued at 505 AM CDT Mon Oct 12 2026

A deep upper trough axis lies over the western CONUS early this
morning, with an embedded closed low over eastern Washington 
and Oregon. Mid level shortwave energy ejecting from the base of
the trough will continue to bring periods of rain across 
western and central North Dakota this morning, diminishing from 
southwest to northeast this afternoon and evening as the 
northern stream begins to cut off from the closed low. The most 
persistent rain is expected in northwest North Dakota, where 
rain could mix with or change over to snow this morning. Latest 
HRRR/RAP soundings at Crosby show maximum temperatures aloft 
remaining above freezing until after sunrise, at which point 
diurnal heating could begin to offset dynamic and evaporative 
cooling mechanisms, keeping surface temperatures just above 
freezing. The most likely outcome is that there will be a few 
hours of a rain/snow mix across Divide and possibly into parts 
of Burke and Williams Counties this morning. Grassy surfaces may
turn white, but the probability of snow accumulations greater 
than half an inch are low.

Forecast highs this afternoon range from the upper 30s 
northwest to around 50 in the southern James River Valley. An 
overcast sky is expected to prevail through the night. This 
will likely prevent a hard freeze, but below freezing 
temperatures are still possible in western and north central 
parts of the state. Broad surface high pressure settles over 
the region on Tuesday ahead of a SW-NE mid level trough axis 
embedded in the northern stream. Deep layer moisture is not 
expected to be sufficient to support any precipitation with the 
mid level trough, except perhaps along the South Dakota border 
where the left exit region of an upper jet could aid forcing for
ascent. Consensus guidance would have low stratus clearing 
Tuesday afternoon and evening, but erosion of stratus is more 
difficult with the lower sun angle this time of year, and flow 
aloft remaining cyclonic does not lend confidence to clouds 
clearing either. Forecast high temperatures in the mid 40s to 
mid 50s may be slightly too warm if/where an overcast sky 
prevails. Confidence does begin to increase in clouds clearing 
Tuesday night, especially in northwest North Dakota where flow 
aloft will begin to turn anticyclonic. NBM 50th percentile lows 
are in the mid 20s to mid 30s at most locations. With surface 
high pressure in place, locations that see a clear sky would 
likely fall colder than this. But even the 90th percentile, 
which would be a more likely outcome under an overcast sky, 
brings Tuesday night lows below freezing across much of western
and north central North Dakota.

Ensemble consensus has increased in a transient upper ridge on 
Wednesday as the cutoff low spins over the Four Corners region 
and the surface high begins sliding eastward toward the Upper 
Mississippi River Valley. A sunnier day should allow high 
temperatures to climb to around 55 to 60, with very light winds.
The forecast from Wednesday night through Friday centers around
the evolution of the Four Corners cutoff low and a potent 
shortwave digging into the southern Canadian prairie provinces 
and US Upper Midwest. Latest cluster analysis gives around a 
75-80 percent chance (3 out of 4 clusters) that the cutoff low 
will eject eastward and interact with the northern shortwave, 
but only around a 15 percent chance (1 of those 3 clusters) it 
will do so far enough west to bring more than some very light 
rain into southern North Dakota Wednesday night into Thursday. 
NBM precipitation chances have in turn lowered to 15-30 percent,
and are only that high from the southwest corner of the state 
to the James River Valley. Regardless of where the phasing of 
the 2 systems occurs, all 3 clusters indicate a potential for 
strong northwest winds on Thursday, with timing of the cold 
frontal passage favorable for maximizing potential momentum 
transfer. Each of the 3 clusters shows medium to high chances 
for 850 mb winds exceeding 40 kts, and low chances for exceeding
50 kts. But there is some longitudinal variability in the axis 
of strongest winds. If the strongest winds were to line up over 
southwest North Dakota, fire weather could become a concern. 

Regardless of the outcome of the cutoff low, ensemble 
confidence is high that strong upper ridging will build over 
the Rockies on Friday and shift eastward on Saturday, leaving a 
quasi-zonal flow pattern over the Northern Plains in its wake. 
Cooler and windy conditions may hold on in eastern parts of the 
region through Friday, but a significant warmup is favored on 
Saturday, with above normal high temperatures in the 60s and 
lower 70s lasting into early next week.
